One of Ember's regional sales teams built an AI process that automates pipeline generation. In six months, the team cut prospecting time by half and now spends that time closing deals.

The COO wants it live in every market by early next year. The other regional sales heads aren't convinced. Three objections keep coming up:
  • "Our sales cycles are longer and relationship-driven."
  • "Our data isn't clean enough for this."
  • "We'd have to drop tools we've already invested in."
The COO has asked for your recommendation.

Ember Group built its reputation on deep expertise, close customer relationships and an entrepreneurial culture. Specialized business units, each with its own systems, leaders and definition of success, serve customers across dozens of regional markets. That structure powered Ember's rise. Now it holds the company back.

Customers demand faster, better and cheaper. AI-native challengers are eroding Ember's edge. Standing still is not an option.

Nearly every unit has started building its own AI solution. The energy is real. So is the mess. Use cases multiply, no one can compare or fund them together, and pilots chase different goals at different speeds.

The question isn't whether AI works. It's whether Ember's leaders can match AI's pace while lifting people up rather than leaving them behind. This moment asks you to be that leader.

A: Tell the working group: "Before we score anything, let's agree how we'll decide." Build criteria together, then score all twelve the same way, your own three included. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "If your case is strong, criteria we all trust will show it."

B: Meet every sponsor, including the one who stayed behind. Ask what each case needs and relies on, then share the patterns with the group before you recommend. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "Help me understand what success looks like for you."

C: Take a view to the CTO: "I think this portfolio has to prove one thing: cost, growth or capability. Which, and is three the right number?" Pause the working group until you agree. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "I want to solve the right problem before I decide where yours fits."

D: Propose to the CTO: two-week trials on five or six cases, with the results choosing the top three before the deadline. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "Let's test it. A strong result is the best argument you can bring."

The Chief Technology Officer has asked you to bring the executive team a recommended portfolio of three funded AI initiatives in four weeks. Your working group has surfaced twelve use cases from across Ember's business units and functions. Each has a sponsor, and several already have polished decks.

No one has agreed on how to decide. Every sponsor believes their case belongs in the top three. Two cases share an executive sponsor who expects both to go forward. After the last session, one sponsor stayed behind: "I've been told this is the highest-value initiative in the portfolio. If it's not in the top three, I need to understand why."

You have a strong view on which three are the real bets. You also know the executive team wants momentum, not another process.

What do you do?

The criteria session is uncomfortable but productive. Sponsors realize they've been defining "value" differently, and the agreed scorecard earns real buy-in. The cost is two of your four weeks, and the criteria miss one case that doesn't fit any category. The shared definition holds, but the executive team asks why speed to value wasn't weighted higher.

Your sponsor conversations reveal that four cases depend on the same data foundation, and two overlap almost entirely. You merge them and your recommendation lands with the group. But sponsors were candid with you and guarded with each other, and a week of meetings leaves less time than you wanted to test the shortlist.

The CTO pushes back on "three initiatives." The real aim is to show the board a credible AI return before year-end, which changes which cases rank. Your reframe saves weeks of debate. But the working group sat idle while you escalated, and several sponsors feel the process moved above their heads.

The trials surface a surprise. The most polished deck stalls on data quality and a modest case delivers results in ten days. The executive team backs the top three on evidence. But two weeks of trials stretched the team thin, and the cases that never got a trial slot feel overlooked.

A: "Yes. There have been leadership conversations about whether to continue the pilot. Nothing is decided, but I want you to know. I've been shielding you and the team from those discussions so you could focus on the work. Given where we are, let's reset milestones together and define what a meaningful win looks like in the next 60 days."

B: Say: "I hear you. I think the team needs a fresh perspective. Let me bring in an AI implementation expert who has helped other teams through similar challenges. They'll join your next meeting, share what's worked elsewhere, and help the team think through where to focus."

C: Say: "The honest answer is that this pilot has run into challenges; more runway won't fix. I want to recommend we document what we've learned, protect the team's reputation, and redirect resources to a higher-confidence initiative. Ember learns through trial and error. I want to make sure you and the team are well positioned for what comes next."

The CFO has named a reporting automation pilot as one of Ember's highest-priority AI initiatives: cut manual reporting time by 35% and improve first-pass accuracy. Your direct report leads the pilot team, and eight people took it on with genuine enthusiasm.

Manual reporting time is down 14%: real progress, but short of the 35% target. The team is running at an unsustainable pace. The CFO has asked for weekly progress reports for six weeks, which the team experiences as surveillance. You've been absorbing the pressure. When your direct report has asked how the CFO feels, you've said the CFO appreciates the effort, which is true but incomplete.

What you haven't shared: the senior leadership team has discussed whether to continue the pilot or redirect resources. Two of the team's strongest contributors are quietly weighing opportunities elsewhere in the company.

Your direct report comes to you: "The team is exhausted. I'm getting the sense the CFO isn't just asking for updates to celebrate us. Is there something I should know?"

What do you do?

Your direct report is apprehensive. The news isn't good, but the uncertainty is gone. You share the context with the team, own the gap between what you said and what you knew, and set two reset milestones. The two contributors considering leaving stay. One later says: "I didn't need it to be easy. I needed to know you were telling us what was real."

The expert is skilled, but their arrival tells the team that leadership doubts them. Your direct report asked a direct question and got outside help instead. The two contributors make their decisions, and trust in you drops. The real problem, a depleted team working without full context, goes untouched.

The framing lands, and the CFO agrees to redirect. The two contributors stay. The pilot closes with a knowledge-capture session. It can be the right call, but works best after an honest look at whether a reset could have worked. Your direct report is left wondering if a different call would have saved the pilot.

A: Acknowledge that the concern is real — and that you share it. Validate the uncertainty without minimizing it. Commit to working through it together and advocate upward for role clarity before the next communication goes out.
B: Be straight: some roles will change — you won't pretend otherwise. Share what's defined, what isn't, and what you're doing to influence it. Commit to a regular cadence of honest updates.

C: Briefly acknowledge the fear, then anchor in why this transformation exists — outcomes for clients, speed for the business, sustainability for the organization. Invite this group to shape how AI gets implemented, positioning them as guides, not passengers.
D: Set the agenda aside. Tell the group the strategy can wait — this can't. Listen without solving. Take notes. Commit to bringing what you hear to leadership before next steps are announced.

Indigo has announced an enterprise-wide AI transformation. Lending and underwriting, wealth management, risk and compliance — significant changes are coming. Leadership has been clear: this is the direction.

You're in what was supposed to be a strategy alignment session with your direct reports — all senior leaders themselves, each managing large teams now asking hard questions.

Before you get through the agenda, one of your most respected peers puts it plainly: "I need to ask you directly — are we being replaced? Because that's the question I can't answer for my people right now." These are experienced leaders — not panicking but watching you closely. They know the initiative is real. Some roles will shift. The full picture isn't defined. And their teams are looking to them for answers they don't have.

What do you do?
Validates the room; these leaders feel seen — increasing their capacity to show up for their own teams. But solidarity without direction can deepen the sense that no one is steering.
Trust-building through honesty. Leaders can handle the truth — and will respect you for it. But naming uncertainty without reassurance can fracture confidence in the initiative, and in you.
Purpose moves people through fear, not around it. But leading with mission before the emotional reality lands can feel like deflection — and leaders notice that.

Creates conditions for real trust. You leave knowing what this group fears — making your advocacy upward specific and credible. But the timeline doesn't pause, and leaders leaving without direction may read it as: the organization doesn't have one.
